head: Encephalitis
Meningitis
visuals.text: Confusion and focal neurology without meningism point to the brain itself.

visuals.title: Working it up
nodes: CSF: lymphocytes, high protein, normal glucose

visuals.title: Do not wait
visuals.text: Aciclovir starts before any result: untreated HSV encephalitis carries high mortality.

visuals.title: How HSV reaches the temporal lobes
nodes: Retrograde spread along trigeminal / olfactory pathways

visuals.title: Where HSV strikes
visuals.text: Travels up cranial nerve pathways to the temporal and frontal lobes.

visuals.title: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
nodes: Target NR1 subunit of NMDA receptor

glossary.Photophobia: Discomfort or pain when looking at light, a sign of meningeal or brain irritation.
glossary.Neck stiffness: Resistance to bending the neck forward, a sign of meningeal irritation.
glossary.Focal neurological deficit: A problem in one part of the nervous system, such as weakness of one limb or speech loss, pointing to a specific brain area.
glossary.Focal neurology: Signs that localise to one part of the nervous system, such as one-sided weakness or speech difficulty.
glossary.Altered mental status: Any change in alertness, thinking or behaviour, from mild confusion to coma.
glossary.Psychosis: Loss of contact with reality, with hallucinations, delusions or disordered thinking.
glossary.Autoimmune: Caused by the immune system attacking the body's own tissues.
glossary.Autoimmune encephalitis: Brain inflammation caused by antibodies against brain proteins rather than by an infection.
glossary.Autoantibody: An antibody that targets the body's own proteins.
glossary.Autoantibodies: Antibodies that target the body's own proteins, here receptors on brain cells.
glossary.HSV-2: Herpes simplex virus type 2, usually genital herpes; a less common cause of encephalitis and meningitis.
glossary.Herpes simplex virus: A common virus that lies dormant in nerves and can reactivate; HSV-1 is the leading cause of viral encephalitis.
glossary.Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis: Widespread inflammatory demyelination of the brain and spinal cord after a viral illness or vaccination.
glossary.Encephalomyelitis: Inflammation of both the brain and the spinal cord.
glossary.Teratoma: A germ cell tumour containing several tissue types, such as hair, teeth or neural tissue.
glossary.Absence-like: Brief episodes of blank staring and unresponsiveness resembling absence seizures.
glossary.Short-term memory: Memory for recent events and new information, held for minutes to days.
glossary.Personality change: A new, lasting shift in behaviour or character noticed by family or friends.
glossary.Seizures: Sudden bursts of abnormal electrical brain activity causing changes in movement, awareness or behaviour.
glossary.Gold standard: The single most accurate test available for confirming a diagnosis.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; detailed scan of soft tissue such as brain, without radiation.
glossary.CT: Computed tomography; fast X-ray cross-sectional scan, often the first brain scan in emergencies.
glossary.Empirical: Treatment started on the most likely cause before test results confirm it.
glossary.Empirically: Treated on the most likely cause before test results confirm it.
glossary.Amoxicillin: A penicillin antibiotic; added in meningitis/encephalitis over 60 to cover Listeria.
glossary.ICU: Intensive care unit, for patients needing organ support or very close monitoring.
glossary.Supportive care: Treatment that keeps the patient safe and stable while the illness settles, rather than curing it.
glossary.Reactivation: A dormant virus becoming active again, often when immunity dips.
glossary.Retrograde spread: Travel of a virus backwards along a nerve axon, from the nerve ending towards the brain.
glossary.Trigeminal: The fifth cranial nerve, carrying sensation from the face; HSV can lie dormant in its ganglion.
glossary.Olfactory: Relating to smell; the olfactory nerve runs from the nose directly into the brain.
glossary.Frontal lobes: The front parts of the brain, controlling personality, behaviour, planning and movement.
glossary.Necrosis: Death of tissue cells from injury or lost blood supply.
glossary.Myelin: The fatty insulating sheath around nerve fibres that speeds up conduction.
glossary.Antigen: A molecule that the immune system recognises and targets.
glossary.Antigens: Molecules that the immune system recognises and targets.
glossary.NMDA receptor: A glutamate receptor on neurons, important in memory and learning.
glossary.Lymphocytes: White blood cells (T and B cells) that dominate in viral and autoimmune inflammation.
glossary.Immunoglobulin: Antibodies; given intravenously (IVIg) as pooled donor antibodies to modulate the immune system.
glossary.Adjunct: An extra treatment added to the main therapy to improve its effect.
glossary.Mortality: The death rate from a disease.
glossary.Flu-like illness: Fever, aches, tiredness and headache resembling influenza, often a viral prodrome.
glossary.Vaccination: Giving a vaccine to train the immune system against an infection.
